title: Open Doors and a Closed One
sum: The Elder writes to his dear friend Gaius. He prays that all goes as well with Gaius as with his soul, and says nothing gives him more joy than hearing that his children walk in truth (1:1-4). Traveling brothers have told the Elder's church how Gaius welcomed them, though they were strangers to him. The Elder asks him to send them on their journey in a way worthy of God: they went out for the sake of the Name and take nothing from pagans, so believers must support them and so share in their work (1:5-8).

One church has done the opposite. Its leading man, Diotrephes, "who loves to be first," rejected a letter from the Elder, speaks against him, refuses to receive the brothers, and drives out of the church those who would. The Elder will deal with it when he comes (1:9-10). Gaius should copy the good, not the bad, and here is a good example: Demetrius, of whom everyone, and the truth itself, speaks well (1:11-12). The Elder has more to say in person; he sends peace and greetings to the friends, each by name (1:13-14).
readings: Read this way, 3 John is a thank-you note and a request: Gaius has done well to receive traveling missionaries, and should keep doing it. Diotrephes is the warning example of a host who shuts his door, and Demetrius, perhaps the letter carrier, is the next traveler to be received. The theme is the same as Jesus' sending of the Twelve: whoever takes in those he sends takes him in (Matthew 10:40; John 13:20).

Read this way, 3 John shows a struggle over who leads the churches. The Elder writes letters and sends envoys; Diotrephes, in his own church, refuses both and enforces his refusal by expelling members. Whether Diotrephes was an early single bishop resisting an older network, or a local strongman, the letter is a rare glimpse of church order being worked out, with no clear rule yet for settling the quarrel.

views.H: Christian travelers depended on believers for lodging and supplies. Letters of recommendation introduced them: a papyrus letter of about AD 25 from Oxyrhynchus introduces "Heraclides, the bearer of this letter" and before its farewell says, "Before all else I pray for your health" (Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 292), a health wish like the one in 3 John 2. The Didache shows churches testing such travelers and sending them on with bread (Didache 11-12).
views.C: The same writer as 2 John, by title, style and ending. The letter is the shortest book of the New Testament in Greek words and the only one that never names Jesus or Christ. Scholars debate who Diotrephes was: Adolf von Harnack (1897) saw in him the earliest monarchical bishop whose name survives; C. H. Dodd saw a quarrel over leadership and authority, not doctrine; John Painter connects it with 2 John. Plummer thought the conduct of Diotrephes was the strongest argument against the apostle's authorship, since it is surprising that anyone would treat the last apostle this way.
views.L: A private letter in the common form: greeting, health wish, joy, request, complaint, commendation, hope of a visit, greetings. It is held together by "truth" (six times), "testify" and "testimony" (five), "beloved" (four) and a set of contrasts: Gaius and Diotrephes, receiving and refusing, the good and the bad.
views.J: Hospitality to strangers was a duty in Israel, from Abraham's tent (Genesis 18) to the saying of Yose ben Yochanan, "Let your house be open wide" (Mishnah Avot 1:5). "The Name" (1:7) is the Jewish way of speaking of God's name (Leviticus 24:11), here used of Jesus. "Peace to you" is the Hebrew greeting shalom.
views.T: A church order of about 380 lists Gaius as bishop of Pergamum and Demetrius as bishop of Philadelphia (Apostolic Constitutions 7.46), and Diotrephes became a byword: the English Puritan John Udall gave his name to a proud bishop in a dialogue of 1588. 3 John 2 has been read as a promise of health and wealth in the prosperity teaching of Oral Roberts and others, and as an ordinary friendly wish by commentators such as Plummer; see the deep dive.

deep.h: Diotrephes and the Elder: what was the quarrel?
deep.b:
All we know is in 1:9-10. Diotrephes "loves to be first" in his church; he does not "welcome" the Elder or his letter; he speaks against him with evil words; he will not receive the traveling brothers; and he stops those who want to, and drives them out of the church. The Elder does not accuse him of false teaching, and not even the place of Diotrephes' church can be told from the letter. Readers explain the conflict in more than one way.

An early bishop. Adolf von Harnack (1897) argued that Diotrephes was the earliest monarchical bishop whose name has survived: a single local leader asserting control over his church against the traveling envoys of an older network led by the Elder. Plummer, earlier, thought Diotrephes wanted to make his church independent of the Elder.

Authority, not doctrine. C. H. Dodd held that the quarrel was about leadership and authority, since the Elder never calls Diotrephes a heretic.

A link with 2 John? Most scholars, Dodd among them, think the letter Diotrephes refused (1:9) was a lost letter, perhaps of recommendation, since 3 John says nothing of the dispute over teaching in 2 John. Plummer agreed that it cannot be 1 or 2 John and thought Diotrephes "would be likely to suppress it." John Painter argues that it was 2 John, pointing to the overlap between 2 John 9 and the hospitality theme of 3 John. If he is right, Diotrephes may have turned 2 John's own rule (2 John 1:10) against the Elder's messengers; that last step is the site's suggestion (see the theory box on the 2 John chapter page), not Painter's.

An awkward fact for tradition. Plummer, who held that the apostle John wrote the letter, admitted that the behavior of Diotrephes "seems to weigh most heavily against the Apostolic authorship," but answered that the New Testament is "full of the saddest surprises": Judas, Peter's denial, the quarrels at Corinth.

In the KJV the verse reads, "Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth." In 1947, Oral Roberts said, his Bible fell open at this verse; the next day, he said, he bought a Buick and God appeared to him, directing him to heal the sick. He began teaching prosperity the same year, and in the 1970s called his teaching on giving "seed faith": a gift was a seed that would grow and come back to the giver.

Three points from the Greek bear on the question. First, peri pantōn means "in every way," not "above all things" (Plummer). Second, the verb translated "prosper" meant to get on well or succeed in general, not to grow rich. Third, the wish for health is the ordinary opening of a Greek letter: "Before all else I pray for your health" (Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 292, about AD 25). The Elder is writing to one friend, not stating a promise for all believers; but his prayer does show that Christians may ask God for health and success for those they love, as Plummer said: "The verse is a model for all friendly wishes of good fortune to others."

deep.title: Claude's theory: why 3 John never names Jesus
deep.b: This is my own reading. 3 John is the only book of the New Testament that never says "Jesus" or "Christ." The one reference to him is "the Name" (1:7). In Jewish speech, "the Name" (Hebrew ha-Shem) stood in for God's own name, which was not spoken aloud (Leviticus 24:11, 16). Acts uses the same phrase for Jesus' name (Acts 5:41). The silence may be simple brevity in a private note. But it may also show how natural it had become, in the Elder's circle, to speak of Jesus with the reverence Jews kept for God's name: the brothers traveled "for the sake of the Name" as Israel was to honor the Name. Plummer notes the Christian use of "the Name" in the early writers; the link with the Jewish reverence for the divine name, as an explanation for the letter's silence, is my own.

settings.to: Gaius, a believer who hosted traveling Christians, probably a convert of the Elder, apparently not a member of Diotrephes' church
settings.when: after traveling brothers returned to the Elder's church and spoke of Gaius' welcome
settings.why: To renew a friendship and praise Gaius before asking more of him. The ordinary letter wish for health is turned into a prayer that his outward life may go as well as his soul. Knowing that this is a private letter keeps verse 2 in proportion: it is a wish for one friend, not a general promise.

settings.when: as the brothers, or a new group, are about to set out again
settings.why: To ask Gaius to keep supplying missionaries who will not take money from pagans. The request turns hospitality into partnership: those who support the travelers become "fellow workers for the truth." Readers who knew Jesus' words about receiving those he sends (Matthew 10:40) would hear their own part in the mission.

settings.to: Gaius, who knows Diotrephes' church but is apparently not under him
settings.when: after Diotrephes refused the Elder's letter and his envoys
settings.why: To explain why Gaius' help is so needed, and to warn him. The Elder promises to bring the matter before the church when he comes, rather than act from a distance. The passage shows a church able to shut its doors and expel members, with no higher court named to decide between it and the Elder.
views: Diotrephes was a single local leader resisting the Elder's network (Harnack).
The dispute was over leadership and authority, not doctrine, since the Elder never calls Diotrephes a false teacher (C. H. Dodd).
The letter Diotrephes refused was 2 John (John Painter); most scholars think it was a lost letter (Dodd; Plummer).

settings.when: probably as Demetrius brings this letter
settings.why: To draw the lesson from the two examples and to introduce Demetrius, who needs a welcome. Three witnesses stand behind him: everyone, the truth itself, and the Elder. In a world without official credentials, this was how a stranger was trusted.

settings.when: as the Elder plans to come soon
settings.why: To end with a promise of a face-to-face talk and with peace. Greeting the friends "each by name" keeps the personal tone of a letter among people who know one another, and ties the small circle around Gaius to the Elder's own.
